questiontext.text: What does BPE training produce from a corpus?

answer.text: The learned merge rules (and resulting vocabulary)

feedback.text: Correct — training discovers which pairs to merge.

answer.text: The attention weights of the model

feedback.text: No — those are learned by the network, not the tokenizer.

answer.text: The final sampled output tokens

feedback.text: No — sampling happens at inference, not tokenizer training.

answer.text: A fixed one-token-per-word dictionary

feedback.text: No — BPE builds subword merges, not whole-word entries.

generalfeedback.text: Training learns the merge rules from the corpus, which together define the vocabulary.

questiontext.text: At each training step, which adjacent symbol pair does BPE merge?

answer.text: The most frequent adjacent pair in the corpus

feedback.text: Yes — the highest-count pair becomes the next new token.

answer.text: The least frequent adjacent pair

feedback.text: No — BPE greedily merges the most common pair.

answer.text: A randomly chosen pair

feedback.text: No — the choice is driven by frequency counts.

generalfeedback.text: Each step counts adjacent pairs and merges the most frequent one into a new token.

questiontext.text: Which best describes one iteration of the BPE training loop?

answer.text: Count adjacent pair frequencies, merge the top pair into a new token, add it to the vocabulary

feedback.text: Yes — count, merge, add, repeat for a fixed number of merges.

answer.text: Delete the rarest token from the vocabulary

feedback.text: No — training adds tokens, it does not prune this way.

answer.text: Sort the corpus and split it into sentences

feedback.text: No — that is not part of the merge loop.

generalfeedback.text: Repeat: count pairs, merge the most frequent, add the new token, for a fixed number of merges.

questiontext.text: Which data structures suit BPE training as described?

answer.text: A max-heap to find the most frequent pair and a linked list for the token sequence

feedback.text: Yes — a priority structure surfaces the top pair; a list represents the sequence.

answer.text: A stack for counting and a queue for merges

feedback.text: No — those do not efficiently surface the most frequent pair.

answer.text: A binary search tree keyed by token length

feedback.text: No — length ordering does not help find the top-count pair.

generalfeedback.text: A max-heap/priority structure finds the most frequent pair; a linked list holds the token sequence.

questiontext.text: Which statements about BPE training are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It merges the most frequent adjacent pair at each step

feedback.text: Yes — greedy by frequency.

answer.text: It repeats for a fixed number of merges

feedback.text: Yes — the merge count is a hyperparameter set in advance.

answer.text: It merges the least frequent pair to save space

feedback.text: No — the most frequent pair is chosen.

answer.text: It never adds new tokens to the vocabulary

feedback.text: No — each merge adds a new token.

generalfeedback.text: Training greedily merges the most frequent pair, adds a new token each time, and repeats for a fixed budget.

questiontext.text: BPE training repeats the merge step for a fixed, pre-set number of merges.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the number of merges is a hyperparameter.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The merge count is fixed in advance.

questiontext.text: BPE training merges the least frequent adjacent pair at each step.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — it merges the most frequent pair.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — the most frequent pair is merged.

questiontext.text: BPE picks the pair to merge based on its adjacency ______ in the corpus.

answer.text: frequency

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: frequent*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: pair

feedback.text: Accepted — the most frequent pair is chosen.
